questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: McGill has good opportunities to try new course material compared with Copenhagen University, and I was intrigued to see how their university education is different from the Danish system. Also, I found it interesting that McGill is located in one of Canada's bilingual regions, and I heard beforehand that Montreal is a very cool place to live.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It was a fantastic experience, and I do not regret it at all, but McGill as a University is maybe not as great as its world ranking. They do not accommodate exchange students very well. Further explained, no regards from McGill were taken to welcome one as a student, so you just have to make friends in class or clubs. 
But how could this have been different, and isn't that the case in all universities? No!
Most universities where I know people go on exchange have welcomed them in some welcoming program, where you can find comfort in other exchange students—examples in Canada are Guelph, Concordia and probably many more.  
McGill does have Frosh, but it is sadly not very well organized if you go to their Macdonald Campus Frosh. But excellent news, if you go to the downtown campus as most people do, you can then participate in the outdoor frosh. Here you will indeed have a great time and avoid the 18-year-old fresh high schoolers :)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
McGill has good sources on their website on how to apply for courses, schedule planners, and when and where to arrive for lectures. So that part went smoothly. Generally, McGill has a lot of information on their website, and all the information is there; sometimes the problem is finding it, but when writing their team for assistance, they are very helpful.
Disclaimer: be prepared to spend some time on the exemption from international health insurance (IHI) McGill has because, as a Danish citizen, you have the right to get RAMQ in Quebec, the same as the Danish yellow health card. Therefore, you can save hundreds of dollars by getting RAMQ, but the system is very old school and takes time to process. 

Also, Minerva is a bit old, but you will use it a lot, so looking at the different themes on the website is beneficial. You can find the exemption from IHI, Schedule Builder, course application, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not receive any assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Again, the welcoming program could be greatly improved, especially since you pay almost 200CA$ for Frosh.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I would not consider it easy; you should look in good time and use the Facebook groups for housing in Montreal. Housing is one of the tricky ones in Montreal. There are a lot of scams in the big Facebook groups and a lot of slumlords, so please be aware of that.
I applied for the McGill residence housing, but as expected, this housing is not likely to go to exchange students (but also not impossible!)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
The apartments in Montreal are old. I was unlucky and lived in a very old apartment where there was a water leakage, and I had to move initially. 
Please have good travelling insurance; I have never been happier for mine!

Despite that, areas to recommend living in that might not be in the McGill ghetto and 5 minutes away from campus, but these areas are gorgeous to live in. Mile End Montreal is the more old part of town, with many cute stores and cafes, it can be compared a bit to Nørrebro or Vesterbro, in my opinion. The plateau is also lovely and closer to McGill downtown. I lived in the McGill ghetto in the first three months because it was close to downtown, where I took the shuttle to the Macdonald Campus, and then I lived my last month in Mile End. I paid around 700CA$ per month downtown and ca. the same in Mile End

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a lot of apartments to rent, but it takes time to find a good scoop. The pricing is okay, and cheap, tidy places exist in Montreal, so please do not be fooled by the 1200CA$ apartments.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: This is a very straightforward process and an excellent guide made by McGill

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You look in the McGill course catalogue for your semester, you build a schedule in the schedule builder in minerva, you apply for the courses in minerva when course registration open.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can always write to someone at McGill for help and emails for the specific problem is linked on McGill official website under courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I applied for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Research the courses beforehand, which you also do when you apply for the pre-approval from UCPH, and take into account that some courses have demands for what previous courses are required for the specific course.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: 3/4 courses I took were great.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took the 200-300 level; the reason behind this was I was limited by a mandatory statistics course, and this was how my schedule could piece together. But 400 and 500 courses are also fine for a bachelor's student. I would not necessarily say that a 200 course is more accessible than a 400 or 500; it depends on the course and how much premature learning you have in the course field. But of course, the 400 and 500 are more specialized courses often.

Sidenote: if you go to the Macdonald's campus, then be aware that the campus is small and there is a limited amount of courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Very different, you call the professor "professor," and lab courses are often seen as a master's student privilege, so I found that a bit peculiar since I'm in Denmark in the lab all the time. 

Overall, it is a learning experience to see how different a university education system can be. Be aware that the view of student responsibility is a lot different than Copenhagen University. My impression is that less is expected of you than UCPH. 

I like, to some degree, that they have a continuous grading system of percentages throughout the semester.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
205 Science Literacy

300 Cropping systems

333 Pollution and bioremediation

310 Statistic methods 1

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
207 Science Literacy is a very good course; it offers a new view of science writing and its importance. Also, it is a very good course to ace the bachelor's or master's thesis because you learn to write well in a structured and captivating manner for the reader. 
From my knowledge, we do not have this as a course on UPCH, which is a shame. Some of the concepts I have been presented at UPCH, but having it as a course creates time for you to master the tools. Science literacy is a 200 course, not necessarily an easy course, but if you engage, then you will pass. 

300 Cropping systems - loved the professor, loved the course material

333 Pollution and bioremediation - I liked the course, and bioremediation is fascinating; also a good way of learning how different handling of wastewater and trash is in Canada.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Simcard is expensive, but I would reccomend the company Fizz.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Transportation is cheap compared to Copenhagen when you are a student. 

Food is a bit more expensive, but this depends on your nearby supermarkets. This somewhat determines your monthly spending since there is a difference in grocery prices in the different areas of Montreal. Not a crazy difference, but maybe a few 100DKK a month.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A lot of clubs to join!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were some, but in my opinion, not many. Also, sometimes overlap with lectures and, therefore, could not attend.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The open-air festival was fun, and International Student Day is a big recommendation, but it is a month into the semester and the only opportunity to meet other international students

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Toronto, Niagara falls, see some national parks etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
The students are a bit hard to approach on a deeper level. I had a lot of friends in the lectures, but outside the lectures, it was hard to connect to the students in my courses. Also keep in mind that one semester (4 months) is also not a lot of time to get to know people. A lot of local social invitations from students in my courses came at the end of my stay.

However, people in Montreal are in general very friendly, so even though I did not have many friends from my courses I saw privately, I did get a lot of friends, and I was very social on my exchange. Sometimes, it is not what you expected but just as great, and that is definitely a take-home from my exchange.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a club and try to find some international students who can relate to your situation. Also, just be friendly and start up a casual conversation. Just take every chance you get to bond with a new person.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I did not find any differences challenging despite their French being very different than European french. French is not a problem at the university because everyone can speak English, and typically, people are very including if you do not speak French. 
The French challenging part is more in your life interacting with locals outside the university.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
Montreal is the most included city I have ever been in regarding gender. I have enjoyed learning what we can do differently in Denmark on this topic. 
Generally, if you are inclusive you get included.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Your exchange success depends on how much effort you put into it
- Be open-minded when meeting new people

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The bars, clubs, karaoke bars and cafes are great, and use them greatly!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people and getting my worldview expanded. Having a break from the Danish rush hour, we do stress too much.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Having to move mid-stay, otherwise, just remember that everything on exchange is just temporary and enjoy it while it last, also on the shitty days.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
